name: Send Your Name to Mars
short_status: Seven spacecraft have put about 22.9 million name entries on the Martian surface, from Pathfinder in 1997 to Perseverance's 10,932,295 in 2021. NASA's page, updated 27 July 2026, says reservations are closed.
tagline: NASA and The Planetary Society · United States · Artefact · 2021 · Multipolar Mars Success
stats: name entries delivered to the Martian surface across seven spacecraft, counting the same person more than once
names on Perseverance's three chips, the largest single delivery
lists that never arrived: Mars 96 in 1996 and Mars Polar Lander in 1999

facts.label: Where it started
facts.value: The Planetary Society put the names of 100,000 of its members on MAPEX, the microelectronics and photonics experiment flown on Mars 96, and mounted MAPEX on the surface of the Visions of Mars compact disc before the package went to Russia. Mars 96 failed on 16 November 1996 and re-entered the atmosphere the next day. A spare MAPEX chip carrying Planetary Society member names flew instead on Mars Pathfinder and landed on 4 July 1997.

facts.label: How many names on Pathfinder
facts.value: The Planetary Society's own mission page says the Pathfinder lander carried the names of over 100,000 of its members on a microchip. Its Messages from Earth catalogue describes the same object as a spare MAPEX chip including member names, without a count. No NASA figure for the Pathfinder names has surfaced in the sources we consulted.

facts.label: The million children
facts.value: Mars Polar Lander carried a CD-ROM of children's names collected under the Send Your Name to Mars banner. Jamais Cascio, writing in Salon on 10 May 1999, says over 932,000 children's names were collected for it and that only school-age children could take part; English Wikipedia rounds the same list to one million. The lander was lost during descent on 3 December 1999 and has never been found.

facts.label: What the 1999 campaign expected next
facts.value: The same Salon piece records that the follow-on campaign, opened to adults, was collecting for the Mars Surveyor 2001 lander and that its programme analyst John Lee expected three to four million names at a minimum. That lander was cancelled in May 2000. NASA's caption for the 2004 rover DVD says it carries nearly four million names collected by NASA in the Send Your Name to Mars project, but we found no source that states the 2001 list was transferred to the rovers, so the connection is suggestive rather than established.

facts.label: The rover DVDs
facts.value: The Planetary Society provided, at no cost to NASA, two identical silica glass DVDs each carrying more than four million names, including every Planetary Society member as of 6 December 2002. They were part of the Red Rover Goes to Mars project and were mounted on the Spirit and Opportunity landers rather than on the rovers themselves, so both discs stayed behind when the rovers drove off. Each also carries dust-collecting magnets and a LEGO astrobot figure at the centre, named Biff Starling on Spirit and Sandy Moondust on Opportunity.

facts.label: The codes on the discs
facts.value: Each DVD has a ring of black dashes around its edge encoding a hidden message. Jim Gillogly of Westwood, California, who had previously cracked part of the Kryptos sculpture at CIA headquarters, solved both once the rovers had photographed them; the Society's release notes he cracked Opportunity's from a NASA image of the disc before the Society had even posted that code. Neither the release nor NASA's caption gives a sol for the photographs. Spirit's reads "Wish you were here" and Opportunity's reads "Explore to learn". The Planetary Society announced the solutions on 15 April 2004.

facts.label: Signatures as well as names
facts.value: Alongside the public name lists, each 2003 rover carried a chip holding about 35,000 laser-engraved signatures collected from visitors to the rovers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, including those of senators, artists and John Glenn. NASA's caption names JPL only; the Kennedy Space Center in its dateline is where the photograph was taken. NASA photographed one before it was fitted to the second rover in April 2003.

facts.label: Phoenix
facts.value: The Planetary Society supplied a silica glass mini-DVD carrying 250,000 names along with the Visions of Mars collection, affixed to the Phoenix lander deck about a metre above the ground. It landed on 25 May 2008 and appears in many of the lander's own images, which makes it the one name deposit on Mars that has been repeatedly photographed in place.

facts.label: Curiosity
facts.value: Two chips the size of a dime, 23 mm across, are fixed to the rover deck carrying 1,246,445 names submitted over a year from 246 countries and territories. About 20,000 visitors to JPL and the Kennedy Space Center also wrote their names on pages that were scanned and reproduced at microscopic scale onto the same chips; NASA's page does not say whether those are counted inside the 1,246,445. The names were written with an electron beam machine in JPL's Microdevices Laboratory at feature sizes below one micron. Fastened to the same chip is a micro-reproduction of Leonardo da Vinci's Codex on the Flight of Birds of about 1505 and his self-portrait.

facts.label: InSight
facts.value: InSight carries two dime-sized silicon chips on its deck. The first, fitted in 2015, holds 826,923 names. The second, fitted on 23 January 2018 and measuring about 8 mm square, holds a further 1.6 million, a figure NASA gives only to two significant figures and rounds with the first chip to a combined total of about 2.4 million names. NASA has not published an exact figure for the second chip in anything we consulted.

facts.label: Perseverance
facts.value: 10,932,295 names were stencilled by electron beam onto three chips the size of a fingernail and installed on the rover at the Kennedy Space Center on 16 March 2020. The chips sit in the upper left corner of a metal plate on the rover's aft crossbeam, within view of the mast cameras, and the same plate carries the essays of the 155 finalists in the Name the Rover contest and a laser-etched image of Earth and Mars joined by the Sun, with the phrase Explore as one written in Morse code in the Sun's rays.

facts.label: Names in Mars orbit
facts.value: MAVEN, which is not a lander, carries a DVD from the Going to Mars campaign holding 96,899 valid names, 1,073 haiku that received at least two public votes out of 12,530 submitted, and all 377 artwork entries. Those three figures come from the campaign page at LASP, which says nothing about the state of the spacecraft; for that see the next fact.

facts.label: The end of MAVEN
facts.value: CBS News, reporting on 3 June 2026, records NASA's announcement that the orbiter could not be recovered and that its mission had ended. The project manager gives the last successful communication as 6 December 2025, when MAVEN failed to transmit after passing behind Mars. NASA expects the spacecraft, and the Going to Mars disc aboard it, to stay in Mars orbit for at least the next 50 to 100 years.

facts.label: The running total
facts.value: Adding the surface deliveries gives about 22,955,663 name entries: over 100,000 on Pathfinder, more than 4,000,000 on each of the two rover landers, 250,000 on Phoenix, 1,246,445 on Curiosity, about 2,426,923 on InSight and 10,932,295 on Perseverance. Those are entries, and entries are not the same as people. The rover DVDs carry identical lists, every Planetary Society member of the day appears on several, and nothing prevents one person entering a campaign more than once, so the number of distinct human beings named on Mars is unknown and materially smaller. The precision is also false at the last few digits: the InSight component is NASA's rounded 1.6 million rather than a counted figure, so treat the total as approximate rather than as a floor.

facts.label: Whether any of it can be read
facts.value: Two different technologies are involved and they age differently. The 1999 CD and the 2004 and 2008 discs store data as digital pits that need a machine and a format to read. The Salon piece of May 1999 reports NASA's position at the time that radiation on the Martian surface would damage the data on the Mars Polar Lander CD beyond recognition within days of landing, and that NASA chose to accept that rather than build shielding. The chips on Curiosity, InSight and Perseverance are different: the names are physically stencilled into silicon at sub-micron scale, so they need a microscope rather than a reader.

facts.label: Status in 2026
facts.value: NASA's Send Your Name to Mars page, updated 27 July 2026, states that reservations are not currently open and that they will reopen closer to a launch date for a future Mars mission. No name-carrying delivery to the Martian surface has happened since Perseverance in February 2021 in anything we could find.

facts.label: How NASA describes the practice
facts.value: JPL's own summary, in December 2020, is that microchips stencilled with names submitted by the public have been carried by all of NASA's landed Mars missions going back to Pathfinder in 1997. That sentence sweeps in Mars Polar Lander, which was a landed mission that failed, and it is the clearest official statement that the practice is now standard rather than occasional.

timeline: Mars 96 fails to leave Earth orbit and re-enters along a track from the eastern Pacific across northern Chile and Bolivia, taking with it MAPEX and the 100,000 Planetary Society member names written on it.
Mars Pathfinder lands in Ares Vallis carrying a spare MAPEX chip with Planetary Society member names, the first list of human names delivered intact to the surface of Mars.

Salon reports that over 932,000 children's names are already aboard the Mars Polar Lander CD and that the newly opened adult campaign, for the Mars Surveyor 2001 lander, expects three to four million more.
Mars Polar Lander is lost during descent near the south polar layered terrain. Its CD of children's names goes with it and has never been located.

A chip with about 35,000 laser-engraved signatures is fitted to each Mars Exploration Rover before launch, and the Planetary Society's two silica glass DVDs, more than four million names apiece, are mounted on the two landers.
Spirit and Opportunity land and photograph their own DVDs within their first days on the surface. Both rovers then drive away, leaving the discs on the lander petals where they remain.
The Planetary Society announces that Jim Gillogly has decoded the hidden messages around the edges of both discs: "Wish you were here" on Spirit's and "Explore to learn" on Opportunity's.
Phoenix lands in the arctic plains with a silica glass mini-DVD on its deck carrying 250,000 names and the Visions of Mars library. It is photographed in place within two days.
Curiosity lands with 1,246,445 names on two dime-sized chips bolted to its deck, written by electron beam at features under one micron, from participants in 246 countries and territories.
A second names chip, holding 1.6 million names, is fitted to the InSight lander deck alongside the 826,923 already flown on the first, for a combined total NASA rounds to 2.4 million.

Three fingernail-sized chips carrying 10,932,295 names and the essays of the 155 Name the Rover finalists are installed on Perseverance's aft crossbeam at the Kennedy Space Center. The rover lands on 18 February 2021.
NASA declares the MAVEN mission over after losing signal on 6 December 2025. The Going to Mars DVD with its 96,899 names stays aboard, in an orbit expected to last another 50 to 100 years.

images.caption: A close-up of a gloved hand holding the small mounted silicon chip that carries about 35,000 laser-engraved signatures collected from visitors to the Mars Exploration Rovers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, photographed before the chip was fitted to the second rover.
The dime-sized mounted microchip carrying 826,923 names submitted by the public, held in a gloved hand in the clean room where the InSight lander was built, before it was affixed to the lander deck.

The anodised placard installed on the aft crossbeam of the Perseverance rover on 16 March 2020, etched with Earth and Mars joined by rays from the Sun, with three fingernail-sized silicon chips fixed in the upper left corner and a leader line labelling them 10,932,295 Explorers.

A close-up of the silica glass DVD on Opportunity's lander, made by the Student Astronauts from three Pancam frames taken through different filters on sol 2, showing the LEGO astrobot figure at the centre, the dust-collecting magnets and the ring of black dashes around the rim that encodes a hidden message.

images.caption: A twenty frame panoramic camera mosaic that Spirit took of its own empty lander, the Columbia Memorial Station, after driving off it on sol 16 in January 2004, showing the open petals, the deflated airbags and the JPL markings. The Planetary Society's caption for the same mosaic notes that the Red Rover Goes to Mars DVD is visible toward the back of the right-hand petal.
